headline: Oil Supertanker Squeeze Is Crimping US Crude Exports, Texas Port CEO Says
author: Christopher Charleston and Nathan Risser

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 12, 2026 at 3:33 PM CST 2 min read

(Bloomberg) -- A shortage of available oil supertankers is constraining US crude exports, prompting shippers to hire smaller vessels and direct more cargoes to Europe, according to the head of the largest US port.

For the first time in four years, not a single very large crude carrier, or VLCC, entered the US Gulf of Mexico to collect an oil cargo last week, Port of Corpus Christi Chief Executive Officer Kent Britton said in an interview with Bloomberg News on Thursday.

The supertanker market has been in disarray since the US-Iran conflict stranded scores of vessels around the Persian Gulf and prompted others to sail circuitous routes to avoid the war zone. With so many of the 2 million barrel-capacity ships charting longer journeys, fewer are available for hire.

Freight rates have soared as a result, hitting a record of almost $80 million per vessel in recent weeks, according to Baltic Exchange data. Although that figure has now dropped to $34 million, it'll need to decline even more before US exporters significantly shift back to the larger ships, Britton said.
At Corpus Christi's port, oil-export terminals are relying on smaller vessels known as Suezmaxes and Aframaxes that are cheaper to hire than VLCCs, according to Britton.
Corpus Christi crude exports fell almost 3% in the third quarter from a year earlier. Despite current freight-market conditions, Britton said it's not permanent.
"They're having to move twice as many ships to get the same amount of oil out, it's just creating a little bit of a bottleneck at the dock," he said
Of the 40 crude cargoes that departed US Gulf Coast ports last week, 17 were bound for Rotterdam while none signaled Asia as their destination, Britton said.
